C.JAL is an RV32C-only instruction that performs the same operation as C.J, but additionally writes the
address of the instruction following the jump (pc+2) to the link register, x1. C.JAL expands to jal x1,
offset.

These instructions use the CR format.

C.JR (jump register) performs an unconditional control transfer to the address in register rs1. C.JR
expands to jalr x0, 0(rs1). C.JR is valid only when rs1≠x0; the code point with rs1=x0 is reserved.

C.JALR (jump and link register) performs the same operation as C.JR, but additionally writes the
address of the instruction following the jump (pc+2) to the link register, x1. C.JALR expands to jalr x1,

0(rs1). C.JALR is valid only when rs1≠x0; the code point with rs1=x0 corresponds to the C.EBREAK
instruction.

results.title: The RISC-V Instruction Set Manual, Volume I: Unprivileged Architecture (version 20250508)
results.text:
2.5. Control Transfer Instructions | Page 31

The indirect jump instruction JALR (jump and link register) uses the I-type encoding. The target
address is obtained by adding the sign-extended 12-bit I-immediate to the register rs1, then setting
the least-significant bit of the result to zero. The address of the instruction following the jump (pc+4) is
written to register rd. Register x0 can be used as the destination if the result is not required.

Plain unconditional indirect jumps (assembler pseudoinstruction JR) are encoded as a JALR with rd=

x0. Procedure returns in the standard calling convention (assembler pseudoinstruction RET) are
encoded as a JALR with rd=x0, rs1=x1, and imm=0.

C.JALR (jump and link register) performs the same operation as C.JR, but additionally writes the
address of the instruction following the jump (pc+2) to the link register, x1. C.JALR expands to
jalr x1, 0(rs1). C.JALR is only valid when rs1̸=x0; the code point with rs1=x0 corresponds

    Strictly speaking, C.JALR does not expand exactly to a base RVI instruction as the value added
    to the PC to form the link address is 2 rather than 4 as in the base ISA, but supporting both
    offsets of 2 and 4 bytes is only a very minor change to the base microarchitecture.

message:
**JALR writes the return address — the address of the instruction following the jump, i.e. `pc + 4` — into its destination register `rd`.** It does *not* write the jump target there; the target is only used to redirect the PC.

Details from the 2025 unprivileged manual:

- "The address of the instruction following the jump (pc+4) is written to register rd." [1]
- The target address itself is computed separately: add the sign-extended 12-bit I-immediate to `rs1`, then force the least-significant bit of the result to zero (so the target is always even, which matters for RVC). [1]
- `x0` may be used as the destination when the return address is not needed — this is how plain indirect jumps (`jr`) and procedure returns (`ret`, encoded as a JALR with `rd=x0`, `rs1=x1`, `imm=0`) are formed. [1]

Compressed variant: `C.JALR` performs the same operation but writes `pc + 2` (the instruction following the 2-byte compressed jump) into the link register `x1`, since it is a 16-bit instruction. [2]

The 2019 manual states the same rule for base JALR — `pc+4` written to `rd`, LSB of the target cleared — so there is no 2019-vs-2025 conflict here; the 2025 text is the current authority. [3] At the assembler level, the pseudoinstruction `jalr rs` means `jalr x1, 0(rs)`, which is the usual "call and link" form that leaves the return address in `x1` (the ABI link register). [4]
